collection.label: Hyperborea: the ancient testimonia
collection.author_name: Greek and Latin writers, 5th c. BCE - 2nd c. AD (medieval manuscripts)
collection.search_terms: hyperborea hyperboreans apollo delos abaris aristeas arimaspians boreas north wind rhipaean
collection.description: What the ancient writers said about the Hyperboreans, the people 'beyond the North Wind' beloved of Apollo, each passage shown on the medieval manuscript page that carries it.

texts.title: Homeric Hymn 7, To Dionysus: the pirates, 'to Egypt or Cyprus or the Hyperboreans'
texts.date_approx: 6th century BCE (probable composition); first half of the 15th century (Leiden BPG 33 H)
texts.source: Leiden, UB, BPG 33 H (M), fol. via Leiden University Libraries (IIIF) + Evelyn-White's Greek and English (1914; Perseus and Project Gutenberg)
texts.description: The seventh Homeric Hymn, Dionysus and the Tyrrhenian pirates, whose master guesses the captive god is bound for Egypt, Cyprus or the Hyperboreans (lines 28-29), on Leiden, UB, BPG 33 H (M), fol..

texts.title: Pindar, Pythian 10.25-44: no road by ship or on foot to the Hyperboreans
texts.source: Vatican, Vat. gr. 1312 (B), fol. via DigiVatLib + Sandys' Greek (Perseus) + D. A. Svarlien's English (Perseus, CC BY-SA)
texts.description: The Hyperborean passage of Pindar's tenth Pythian ode (498 BCE): Perseus feasting with them, their music, and their life without sickness, age or toil (lines 25-44), on the 12th-century manuscript Vat. gr. 1312, fol. 164v-165v.

texts.title: Pindar, Olympian 3: Heracles brings the olive from the land of the Hyperboreans
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 32.52 (D), fol. via Teca digitale BML + Sandys' Greek (Perseus) + D. A. Svarlien's English (Perseus, CC BY-SA)
texts.description: Pindar's third Olympian ode (476 BCE), in which Heracles fetches the wild olive for Olympia from the Hyperboreans who serve Apollo, on the manuscript Laur. Plut. 32.52, fol. 6v-7v.

texts.title: Herodotus, Histories 4.13-16: Aristeas of Proconnesus, the Arimaspians and the Hyperboreans
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 70.3 (Herodotus A, 10th c.) fol. 150r-151r via Teca digitale BML + Godley's Greek (Perseus) + Macaulay's English (1890, Project Gutenberg)
texts.description: Herodotus on the poet Aristeas of Proconnesus, who placed the Hyperboreans beyond the one-eyed Arimaspians and the gold-guarding griffins (Histories 4.13-16), on the 10th-century manuscript Laur. Plut. 70.3, fol. 150r-151r.

texts.title: Herodotus, Histories 4.32-36: the Hyperboreans and their offerings to Delos
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 70.3 (Herodotus A, 10th c.) fol. 154r-155v via Teca digitale BML + Godley's Greek (Perseus) + Macaulay's English (1890, Project Gutenberg)
texts.description: Herodotus' chapters on the Hyperboreans: their sacred offerings wrapped in wheat straw, the maidens Hyperoche, Laodice, Arge and Opis who came to Delos, and Abaris with his arrow (Histories 4.32-36), on Laur. Plut. 70.3, fol. 154r-155v.

texts.title: Callimachus, Hymn to Delos 275-299: the offerings of the Hyperboreans
texts.source: Paris, BnF, grec 2763, fol. 79v-80v via Gallica (BnF) + Wilamowitz's Greek (1897, Perseus) + A. W. Mair's English (1921)
texts.description: Callimachus on the first-fruits sent to Delos by the Hyperboreans, 'a very long-lived race', and the daughters of Boreas who first brought them (Hymn 4.275-299), on Paris, BnF, grec 2763, fol. 79v-80v.

texts.title: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 4.592-626: the Eridanus, amber, and Apollo's tears among the Hyperboreans
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 32.9 (L), fol. 249r-249v via Teca digitale BML + Mooney's Greek (Perseus) + Seaton's English (1912, Project Gutenberg)
texts.description: The Argonauts enter the Eridanus, where the Heliades weep amber; the Celts say these are the tears Apollo shed when he went to the sacred race of the Hyperboreans (Argonautica 4.592-626), on Florence, Laur. Plut. 32.9 (L), fol. 249r-249v.

texts.title: Diodorus of Sicily, Library 2.47: Hecataeus on the Hyperboreans, their island and Apollo's round temple
texts.source: Vat. gr. 130 via DigiVatLib + Vogel's Greek (Perseus) + Oldfather's English (Loeb 1935, LacusCurtius)
texts.description: Diodorus' account, after Hecataeus of Abdera, of the Hyperboreans' island beyond the land of the Celts, with its precinct and round temple of Apollo (Library 2.47), on Vat. gr. 130.

texts.title: Strabo, Geography 1.3.22: Eratosthenes, Herodotus and the Hyperboreans
texts.source: Paris, BnF, grec 1397 (Strabo A) fol. 34v via Gallica (BnF) + Meineke's Greek (Perseus) + Hamilton and Falconer's English (1854-1857, Perseus)
texts.description: Strabo reports Eratosthenes' reply to Herodotus' remark that if there are Hyperboreans there must be Hypernotians (Geography 1.3.22), on the manuscript Paris gr. 1397, fol. 34v.

texts.title: Strabo, Geography 7.3.1: ignorance of the north and the tales of the Rhipaean mountains and the Hyperboreans
texts.source: Paris, BnF, grec 1397 (Strabo A) fol. 155v-156r via Gallica (BnF) + Meineke's Greek (Perseus) + Hamilton and Falconer's English (1854-1857, Perseus)
texts.description: Strabo on the lands beyond the Elbe and the Danube, where ignorance gave credit to the fables of the Rhipaean mountains and the Hyperboreans (Geography 7.3.1), on Paris gr. 1397, fol. 155v-156r.

texts.title: Strabo, Geography 11.6.2: the northern peoples whom earlier writers called Hyperboreans
texts.source: Paris, BnF, grec 1393 (Strabo C) fol. 132v via Gallica (BnF) + Meineke's Greek (Perseus) + Hamilton and Falconer's English (1854-1857, Perseus)
texts.description: Strabo on the peoples around the Caspian, and the older Greek writers who called those above the Euxine, the Danube and the Adriatic Hyperboreans (Geography 11.6.2), on Paris gr. 1393, fol. 132v.

texts.title: Strabo, Geography 15.1.57: Megasthenes' marvels and the thousand-year Hyperboreans
texts.source: Paris, BnF, grec 1393 (Strabo C) fol. 207v via Gallica (BnF) + Meineke's Greek (Perseus) + Hamilton and Falconer's English (1854-1857, Perseus)
texts.description: Strabo rejects the marvels Megasthenes told of India, among them the Hyperboreans who live a thousand years, as Simonides and Pindar also said (Geography 15.1.57), on Paris gr. 1393, fol. 207v.

texts.title: Pomponius Mela, Chorographia 3.36-37: the Hyperboreans under the pole
texts.source: Vatican Library, Vat. lat. 4929 (9th c.) fol. 179v-180r via DigiVatLib + Frick's Latin (Teubner 1880) + Golding's English (1585, EEBO-TCP)
texts.description: Pomponius Mela's description of the Hyperboreans (Chorographia 3.36-37), on the 9th-century manuscript Vat. lat. 4929, the only independent witness to his work, with Frick's Latin and Arthur Golding's English of 1585.

texts.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 4.88-91: the Rhipaean mountains and the Hyperboreans
texts.source: Leiden, UB, VLF 4 (Pliny A, 8th c.) fol. 27r-27v + Mayhoff's Latin (Perseus) + Bostock and Riley's English (1855, Perseus)
texts.description: Pliny the Elder on the Hyperboreans beyond the north wind (Natural History 4.88-91), on the 8th-century Northumbrian manuscript Leiden VLF 4, fol. 27r-27v, with Mayhoff's Latin and Bostock and Riley's English.

texts.title: Pausanias, Description of Greece 1.31.2: the route of the Hyperborean first-fruits to Delos
texts.source: Paris gr. 1410 via Gallica (BnF) + Spiro's Greek (Perseus) + Jones's English (Loeb, Perseus)
texts.description: Pausanias on the first-fruits of the Hyperboreans, passed by the Arimaspi, Issedones and Scythians to Sinope and through Greece to Prasiae in Attica, and taken by the Athenians to Delos (1.31.2), on Paris gr. 1410.

texts.title: Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.5.7-10: the Delphic oracle founded by men from the Hyperboreans
texts.source: Paris gr. 1410 via Gallica (BnF) + Spiro's Greek (Perseus) + Jones's English (Loeb, Perseus)
texts.description: Pausanias on Boeo's hymn, which said the oracle at Delphi was founded by Hyperboreans, Olen first among them, and on the temple of wax and feathers sent by Apollo to the Hyperboreans (10.5.7-10), on Paris gr. 1410.

authors.name: Pomponius Mela
authors.bio: Roman geographer from Tingentera in southern Spain, author of the Chorographia, the oldest surviving Latin geography.

authors.name: Callimachus
authors.bio: Poet and scholar of Cyrene who worked at the library of Alexandria; author of hymns, epigrams and the Aetia.
